facts.statement: Scaniacypselus lived during the Eocene epoch in Denmark, Germany, and France.
facts.quote: Scaniacypselus is an extinct genus of basal swifts from the Eocene of Denmark, Germany and France.

facts.statement: Many well-preserved specimens of Scaniacypselus with preserved plumage were found in the Messel Pit near Darmstadt, Germany.
facts.quote: Many well preserved specimens still showing plumage were discovered in the Messel Pit near Darmstadt, Germany.

facts.statement: Scaniacypselus species had broader wings than modern swifts and hindlimbs adapted for perching on tree branches.
facts.quote: Species of Scaniacypselus had relatively broader wings than modern swifts and hindlimbs better adapted to perching on tree-branches

facts.statement: The first remains of Scaniacypselus were recovered by D.J. Ward from the Røsnæs Clay in Denmark.
facts.quote: The first remains of Scaniacypselus were recovered by D.J. Ward from the Røsnæs Clay in Denmark.

facts.statement: The type species S. wardi is known only from a single, almost complete left wing specimen.
facts.quote: The type and only known specimen of S. wardi is an almost complete left wing.

facts.statement: The species S. szarskii was originally described by Peters in 1985 as a species of Aegialornis from the Messel Pit in Germany.
facts.quote: The second species, Scaniacypselus szarskii, was originally described as a species of Aegialornis by Peters in 1985 from the sediments of the Messel Pit in Germany.

facts.statement: Mayr and Peters transferred S. szarskii to the genus Scaniacypselus in 2001 based on an additional specimen.
facts.quote: The species was referred to Scaniacypselus in 2001 by Mayr and Peters on the basis of an additional specimen.

facts.statement: The genus name Scaniacypselus combines the Latin name of the region where the type species was found with the old name Cypselus for the common swift.
facts.quote: The name derives from the Latin name of the region the type species was found in combined with "Cypselus", an old name of the common swift.

facts.statement: The type species S. wardi possessed a short and stout humerus similar to that of modern swifts.
facts.quote: The type species, S. wardi, was noted to have had a short and stout humerus similar to modern swifts.

facts.statement: The ulna of S. wardi was relatively short and stout but more slender than in modern swifts.
facts.quote: The ulna was likewise relatively short and stout, however still more slender than what can be observed in extant forms.

facts.statement: S. szarskii had a relatively longer ulna and shorter carpometacarpus compared to modern swift relatives.
facts.quote: Scaniacypselus szarskii also differs notably in the proportions of the wings, with a relatively longer ulna and shorter carpometacarpus than its modern relatives.

facts.statement: The tarsometatarsus of Scaniacypselus was highly reduced but more resembled that of treeswifts than modern swifts.
facts.quote: The tarsometatarsus (lower leg) of Scaniacypselus is highly reduced but bears more resemblance to treeswifts.

facts.statement: The feet of Scaniacypselus were anisodactyl, with three toes facing forward and one facing backward.
facts.quote: The feet are described as anisodactyl, meaning that three toes face forward while one faces back.

facts.statement: The tail feathers of Scaniacypselus were only lightly forked.
facts.quote: The tail feathers of Scaniacypselus was only lightly forked.

facts.statement: Unlike highly aerial true swifts, Scaniacypselus lived a much less airborne life.
facts.quote: While true swifts are highly aerial animals that spend most their lifes in the air, Scaniacypselus lived a much less airborne life.

facts.statement: Mayr classified Scaniacypselus as a basal member of the family Apodidae rather than the subfamily Apodinae.
facts.quote: Mayr subsequently recovers Scaniacypselus not as a member of the family Apodinae, but instead as a more basal member of Apodidae.

facts.statement: It is debated whether the incision on the sternum of Scaniacypselus has a specific function, as it appears inconsistently across specimens.
facts.quote: The nature of this incision is however not entirely understood, as it is only present in some specimens and not others.
